newsitem.title: USA: Flood danger remains high as California counts cost.
newsitem.headline: Flood danger remains high as California counts cost.

text.p: Broad swaths of prime California farmland were under water and danger of new flooding remained high on Monday as officials began assessing damage from storms and floods in the western United States.

At least 1,250 homes have been damaged by the California floods and thousands of acres of land remained inundated in Yuba and Sutter counties north of Sacramento and in the Modesto area in the state's fertile central valley.

Workers battled to hold back floods from the small northern California town of Meridian while in Yosemite National Park, officials planned to evacuate 500 park workers because of a dwindling water supply and failed sewage system.
California was among states hard hit by fierce storms last week that killed more than 20 people and caused hundreds of millions of dollars of damage in five western states.

The upper Midwest was also reeling from extreme weather on Monday. Residents of the region hauled away gigantic snowdrifts using heavy construction equipment after a weekend blizzard closed roads and stranded travelers. At least four fatalities were blamed on the storm.
Wisconsin residents used front-end loaders to tackle the huge drifts and North Dakota road crews called for a snowblower to tackle a huge mound of snow that cut off normally busy Interstate 29.
California Gov. Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency in four more counties on Sunday, bringing the area covered by his emergency proclamation to 41 of the state's 58 counties.
President Bill Clinton has declared a major disaster in parts of California, Idaho and Nevada hit by floods and mudslides, making federal aid available to flood victims.
James Lee Witt, director of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, arrived in California on Monday to tour flood-ravaged areas.

Officials were only starting to assess the damage but preliminary losses in just six flood-hit counties were estimated at $50 million. Officials say losses to farmers in America's No. 1 agricultural state could be high.
Dozens of levees gave way and others were weakened by raging rivers swollen by last week's storms and heavy runoff from melting snow in the mountains.

But tens of thousands of evacuees were able to return to their homes in Yuba City and Marysville near Sacramento at the weekend and only about 3,800 people remained in 25 shelters, the state Office of Emergency Services said.

On Monday, concern focused on land bordering the delta east of San Francisco where the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers flow into San Francisco Bay. Freda Radich, spokeswoman for the California Office of Emergency Services, said the delta continued to be "stressed" by very high water levels.

"The potential for loss of levees will increase through Tuesday as additional flows arrive and levees become more saturated. Some of the highest tides of the year will occur this week which will put additional pressure on the delta levee system," she said.

Near Meridian, 50 miles (80 kms) north of Sacramento, about 200 people worked around the clock to build a 10-foot (3-metre) high earth wall around the town to hold back gradually rising floodwaters after a levee on a nearby river broke, flooding an estimated 40 square miles (104 square kilometres) of farmland.

The workers were putting the finishing touches to the barrier on Monday just as floodwater began lapping at it. Officials had fingers crossed that the wall would stop floodwater, which could go as high as four feet (120 cms), from flooding the town's 200 houses. The 400 residents have been evacuated.

"We're really confident. We put a lot of effort into this. We really think it's going to work," said Steve Robertson, a spokesman for the California Department of Forestry, which is helping with the flood fight.

Officials at California's scenic Yosemite National Park, battered by the storms, said they would evacuate 500 park employees and their families who live in the park because of a failed sewage system and declining drinking water supplies.

The employees, who work at hotels and lodges in the park, were to drive out, but park spokeswoman Ginger Burley said the plan was on hold for now because fallen trees had closed the only road out of the park that had been reopened.
The park said a second phase of the evacuation might be needed in which all government employees and their families not involved in cleanup work would have to leave.

Yosemite, which has more than 4 million visitors a year, was closed to tourists and could remain closed for weeks, Burley said. Park facilities, bridges and roads were badly damaged and large stretches of highway were "completely gone," she said. "There will even be decisions about how much gets rebuilt," she added.
